title: The Force of the Threatened Attack
subtitle: Turn a threat against the king into lasting pressure

source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter IV, §22 The Force of the Threatened Attack, Example 52

steps.title: A central outpost
steps.source: Played at the Havana International Masters Tournament, 1913. French Defence. White J. R. Capablanca. Black R. Blanco.

narration.say: Capablanca plays White against Blanco. The game begins with the French Defence.
White develops a knight. Black exchanges in the centre, and White recaptures.
Both sides develop another knight. White exchanges on f6.
Knight to e5. Capablanca wants to discourage Black's usual bishop development through b7.
This moves the same knight again before development is complete. Capablanca acknowledges the exception and explains its purpose.
Black develops the bishop to d6. White brings the queen to f3, and Black plays c6.
Capablanca criticises c6: Black missed the more active central challenge c5.
White supports the centre with c3. Black castles, and White develops the bishop to g5.
Black retreats the bishop to e7. White develops the other bishop to d3, and Black retreats the knight to e8.
White's pieces are ready to threaten the king. Black has spent time retreating instead of finding active play.

steps.title: Make Black change the pawn shelter

narration.say: The bishop on d3 points toward h7. Bring the queen to the h-file to increase the pressure.

exercise.prompt: Follow Capablanca's plan: move the queen to h3.

feedback.*: The queen can move from f3 to h3. It joins the pressure against the king's shelter.

exercise.success: 12. Qh3. Black answers with f5, stopping the direct attack but creating a weakness.

steps.title: The threat has earned something lasting
steps.source: White has no longer an attack, but has compelled Black to create a marked weakness. Now White's whole plan will be to exploit this weakness—the weak e Pawn.

narration.say: The pawn on f5 blocks the bishop's diagonal. White must change plans rather than insist on the old attack.
Black's e6-pawn is the new target. White exchanges bishops and castles.
The rook from f1 comes to e1. Black brings the knight to d6.
Rook to e2. Black develops the bishop to d7, and White doubles rooks on the e-file.
Black puts the other rook on e8. White advances c4, and Black brings the knight to f7.

steps.title: Find a new way to increase the pressure

narration.say: Black has assembled defenders around e6. White now opens the centre with the d-pawn.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Advance the d-pawn to break open the centre.

feedback.*: Push the pawn from d4 to d5. White opens new lines while Black's pieces are occupied with defence.

exercise.success: 19. d5! Black exchanges the knight on e5.

narration.say: The rook takes the knight on e5. Black plays g6, and White brings the queen to h4.
Black moves the king to g7. Queen to d4 increases the pressure, and Black challenges the centre with c5.
Queen to c3. Black plays b6. White takes on e6, and the bishop retreats to c8.
White's pieces have freedom to manoeuvre. Black's pieces are occupied with the central defence.

steps.title: The bishop finds a stronger diagonal
steps.source: 25.Be2! The deciding and timely manoeuvre. All the Black pieces are useless after this Bishop reaches Bd5.

narration.say: The bishop on d3 can become much stronger on d5. Start the route through e2 and f3.

exercise.prompt: Begin the bishop manoeuvre: move it to e2.

feedback.*: Retreat the bishop from d3 to e2. The retreat prepares a stronger post on d5.

exercise.success: 25. Be2! A retreat with an attacking purpose.

narration.say: Bishop to f3. Black moves the king to f7, and the bishop arrives on d5.
Black moves the queen to d6. White brings the queen to e3, and Black shifts a rook to e7.
White has reached the position Capablanca wanted. Black's pieces are tied to defence, while White can prepare another threat.

steps.title: Bring the h-pawn into the plan

narration.say: Queen to h6. Black returns the king to g8.
White advances the h-pawn to h4. Black plays a6, and White pushes on to h5.
Black plays f4. White exchanges on g6, disrupting the pawn shelter.
The rook takes the bishop on e6. Black resigns.
The direct attack did not need to succeed immediately. Its threat forced a weakness, and White kept improving the pressure until the defence collapsed.

steps.title: A threat can be stronger than its execution
steps.source: For, holding the threat in hand, forces the opponent to provide against its execution and to keep material in readiness to meet it.

narration.say: First, threaten the king. When Black weakens e6 to defend, change the target.
Double rooks, open the centre, and improve the bishop. Keep your pieces free while your opponent's pieces remain tied down.
Finally, create another threat against the king. The defender must answer threats in more than one place.
